analysis.one_liner: Bans online ads targeted using a person's browsing history and other personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies from deciding which ads to show you based on your browsing history, the contents of your messages, or other data tied to you or your devices. Ads based on what you are currently viewing or searching, or on your general location, would still be allowed. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals could sue to enforce the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, whose browsing history, communications, and device data would no longer be collected and used to target ads at them. The bill also lets individuals sue violators for $100 to $5,000 per violation and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements, so people could take claims to court instead of arbitration. People in protected classes — race, religion, sex, disability and others — would get extra protection, since ads could not be targeted using data that identifies them as members of those groups [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits advertising facilitators (platforms, ad networks, and data brokers paid to deliver ads) from targeting ads using personal information such as browsing history, communications content, or unique device identifiers [S2][S3].
Bars advertisers from targeting ads with data purchased from third parties or with data that identifies someone as a member of a protected class like race, religion, sex, or disability [S2][S3].
Keeps advertising possible without personal tracking: ads matched to the content a person is viewing or searching, and ads based on geography, remain allowed [S2][S3].

Gives individuals a private right to sue with statutory damages of $100-$5,000 per violation, voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these disputes, and lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the ban [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The digital advertising industry — ad platforms, ad exchanges, and data brokers — whose business of collecting personal data and selling targeted ad placement would be curtailed. Advertisers, including small businesses that rely on precise targeted ads to reach customers, would lose that tool and could face higher, less efficient advertising costs [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban goes beyond the biggest platforms: any advertiser or paid ad distributor using personal data to pick an audience is covered, so small businesses and publishers that rely on targeted ads to reach customers and fund free content would bear real costs [S3].

The private right of action allows statutory damages of $100-$1,000 per negligent violation and $500-$5,000 per willful violation, with no requirement to show actual harm beyond the violation itself, which could generate large class-action litigation against a wide range of companies [S3].

Contextual and geographic targeting would still be legal, so data collection around advertising would not stop entirely; the economics of free, ad-supported websites would have to adjust, and some sites might charge subscription fees instead [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: ordinary users would stop having their browsing and communications turned into advertising dossiers, at the cost of less precise advertising for businesses and an unknown hit to ad-funded free content. The per-violation private right of action is aggressive and could be abused in litigation, and one-attribution details (like which data counts as 'reasonably linkable' to a person) would have required FTC rulemaking to settle. But the bill was written to preserve contextual and location-based ads, so it targets the surveillance part of the business rather than advertising itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote on it, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on January 19, 2022 [S1][S5].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the only committee action it ever received [S1][S5].
It drew a single cosponsor, one Democrat, and no Republican support [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital advertising platforms, ad exchanges, and data brokers keep their existing business of collecting personal data and selling targeted ad placement, and ordinary users remain subject to that tracking.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a ban on targeted surveillance advertising

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: Digital advertising industry
against.role: Platforms, ad exchanges, and data brokers that sell targeted advertising
against.what_they_did: Had the most to lose from a ban on targeted ads built on personal data; the bill's core business would have been curtailed

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the only support was from Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and no Republican ever signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Digital advertising and adtech (platforms, ad networks, data brokers)
industries.note: These firms are paid to deliver ads and collect or process the personal data used to target them; the bill would bar that targeting and even bar handing over device lists or identifiers to advertisers. Its profits come from tracking people whose data they use, which is exactly what the bill stops [S3].

Their business is assembling 'reasonably linkable' personal data — browsing history, device identifiers, inferences — and selling it; the bill prohibits advertisers from targeting with purchased data and facilitators from using it [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Advertisers, including small businesses relying on targeted ads
industries.note: They would lose precise targeting and likely pay more for less efficient advertising, but they would also gain protection from data purchased from brokers and from discriminatory ad targeting by protected class [S3].
They would keep contextual ads (matched to the page a user is viewing) but could lose higher-paying personalized ads, pressuring some toward subscriptions or other revenue models [S3].
